papers.title: A deep causal inference model for interpretable travel behaviour analysis
papers.journal: Transportation Research Part C Emerging Technologies
papers.abstract: Transportation policy assessment often involves causal questions, yet traditional travel behaviour lacks the ability of distinguishing causal association from non-causal correlations. We present the deep CAusal infeRence mOdel for traveL behavIour aNAlysis (CAROLINA) , a novel framework that addresses both observed and unobserved confounders in discrete choice modelling through causal discovery and the strengths of deep neural networks. Within this interpretable framework, we also introduce a Generative Counterfactual model for forecasting individuals’ behaviour by adapting the Normalizing Flow method. Through the case studies of virtual reality-based pedestrian crossing behaviour, revealed preference travel behaviour from London, and synthetic data, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models in isolating causal relationships from confounding associations. Our proposed causal framework enhances predictive accuracy by employing data-driven algorithms, while maintaining interpretability. In addition, the counterfactual results show that intervention mechanisms that can reduce pedestrian stress levels lead to a 35.35% increase in individuals experiencing shorter waiting times. External interventions that reduce travel distances of non-mandatory trips in London lead to a 47% increase in the possible use of active and public transit modes.

papers.title: Seven myths about causal inference in ecology: clarifications and common ground

author_details.name: Katherine Siegel
affiliations: Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences

author_details.name: Tyler L. McIntosh
affiliations: Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences

papers.abstract: Identifying and quantifying causal relationships from data is a central goal in ecology and conservation. To achieve this goal, ecologists are increasingly applying frameworks and methods from the broader, multidisciplinary causal inference literature. These applications have generated both enthusiasm and skepticism. Here, we address seven common sources of skepticism that we see as myths. Much of this skepticism treats causal inference as a competing research paradigm. However, it is better understood as a set of ideas and practices that can sharpen ecological reasoning and strengthen empirical evidence. The value of causal inference lies in clarifying the assumptions required to interpret statistical associations causally and in encouraging researchers to state these assumptions explicitly, justifying them using prior knowledge and biological reasoning. In this sense, causal inference does not replace what ecologists already do well. Rather, it helps reveal, refine, and communicate the logic already underlying empirical research with causal aims. Across the seven concerns that we examine, a common message emerges: debates about causal inference should focus less on labels and techniques and more on whether the assumptions behind a causal claim are credible, clearly stated, and fit for purpose when making causal claims in ecology.

papers.title: Causal inference with real-world data in health care research: a scoping review protocol and study within a review protocol
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study will improve the understanding and application of causal inference methods in health care research using real-world data (RWD). It seeks to systematically synthesize existing methods across different data sources, and assess whether large language models (LLMs) can support key steps in review processes. INTRODUCTION: Randomized controlled trials are considered the gold standard for evaluating treatment effects, as randomization balances confounders and enables causal inference. However, randomized controlled trials are often costly, time-consuming, or ethically infeasible. As a result, RWD, such as electronic health records, medical registries, and health insurance claims, are increasingly used in medical research. Complex methods are necessary to derive causal inference from RWD. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Studies that use RWD, evaluate any type of health outcome as a primary endpoint in order to investigate patient health status, address a causal question related to a treatment or intervention, and estimate a causal effect size related to the causal question will be eligible for inclusion. METHODS: PubMed, Embase.com, and Web of Science will be searched for articles published in peer-reviewed journals between January 1, 2010, and January 29, 2026. A scoping review will be conducted to identify and categorize causal inference methods applied to RWD, focusing on theoretical frameworks, data requirements, and inferential assumptions in order to develop a taxonomy of methods. The frequency, context of use, and quality of reporting will be systematically assessed. In parallel, a study within a review (SWAR) will evaluate the performance of LLMs for title and abstract screening and full-text data extraction compared with human reviewers. REVIEW REGISTRATION: OSF https://osf.io/69mcd; SWAR Store (ID 66) https://www.qub.ac.uk/sites/TheNorthernIrelandNetworkforTrialsMethodologyResearch/FileStore/SWARFileStore/SWAR66%20Stella%20Erdmann%20(2025%20AUG%2001%202302).pdf.

papers.title: Minimax designs and estimators for causal inference under network interference
papers.abstract: We develop a design-based minimax theory for linear causal estimands under interference. We study the minimax risks of three problems: optimizing an estimator under a fixed design, optimizing an estimator and a design from a restricted class, or optimizing both over all designs. In each problem, we study the minimax risk over all estimators and over design-unbiased estimators separately. We allow any correctly specified exposure mapping, including the identity. Our theory represents causal inference under interference as a constrained sampling design on an expanded finite population of $\sum_i d_i$ potential outcomes, where $d_i$ is the number of exposure levels attainable by unit $i$. We describe the constrained sampling design by a weighted sampling hypergraph: its vertices are the potential outcomes, its hyperedges are the maximal sets of potential outcomes that can be jointly sampled under feasible treatment assignments, and its weights are induced by the randomization design. We show that the minimax risks of the fixed-design, restricted-design, and all-design problems depend, respectively, on the weighted hypergraph induced by the design, the collection of weighted hypergraphs attainable within the restricted class, and the unweighted hypergraph. Our Bayes lower bounds compare potential-outcome tables that differ on jointly missing sets of potential outcomes: joint-missingness probabilities govern the lower bounds over all estimators, whereas the corresponding odds govern the lower bounds over unbiased estimators. We illustrate the theory for average treatment effects without interference, saturation designs under partial interference, total, direct, and contagion effects under neighborhood interference, and bipartite dose-response contrasts. The upper and lower bounds match in several settings.

papers.title: Doubly-robust causal inference for multi-valued treatment regimes with recurrent neural networks
papers.abstract: We propose a doubly-robust method to estimate the causal effects of multi-valued treatment regimes on patient outcomes. A multi-valued treatment regime assigns personalized treatments from a set of competing options based on a patient's history. Existing methods for optimal treatment regimes are largely limited to binary or continuous treatments. We extend the longitudinal targeted minimum loss-based estimator (LTMLE) to accommodate multi-valued treatments by modeling treatment assignments with a multinomial model. We further integrate recurrent neural networks (RNNs) into the LTMLE framework as learners for the outcome, treatment, and censoring models, and compare this approach to ensemble machine learning. Simulation studies show that LTMLE with either ensemble machine learning or RNNs is approximately unbiased, with close to nominal coverage, whereas sequential g-computation with ensemble machine learning is substantially biased under a dynamic rule. A multinomial treatment model performs similarly to a series of binomial regressions with ensemble machine learning, but yields more stable inference when the treatment model is an RNN.

papers.title: Genetic-multi-omics causal inference coupled with integrative in-vitro toxicology reveals immune-metabolite mediators for aortic aneurysm risk
papers.abstract: Objective Aortic aneurysm (AA) is a life-threatening vascular disease characterized by immune disturbance and metabolic dysregulation. Multi-omics-driven precision toxicity prediction, integrating human genetic causal inference with functional in-vitro toxicology, remains under-explored for uncovering metabolite mediators underlying AA disease risk.This study aimed to dissect metabolite-dependent causal pathways linking immune cells to AA, and evaluate dose-response cytotoxicity of key mediating metabolites toward vascular cells. Methods Two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR) and two-step mediation analysis were performed using European-ancestry GWAS summary datasets covering 731 immune-cell traits, 1,091 plasma metabolites, 3,230 AA cases and 475,964 controls. Complementary in-vitro CCK-8 cytotoxicity experiments on human aortic smooth muscle cells (HASMCs) were further conducted for candidate metabolites Adrenate (22:4n6) and BAFF-R. Results BAFF-R on CD20 − (OR = 0.859, 95%CI: 0.797–0.926, P = 7.17 × 10 −5 ) and, to a lesser extent, Granulocyte AC (OR = 0.900, 95%CI: 0.843–0.961, P = 1.57 × 10 −3 ) emerged as candidate protective immune-cell markers for AA. Adrenate (22:4n6) and Nisinate (24:6n3) mediated 4.47% and 9.84% of these protective effects, respectively. Adrenate triggered significant dose-dependent cytotoxicity in HASMCs. Conclusion This multi-omics genetic-toxicology study provides causal genetic evidence for immune-metabolite regulatory axes in AA pathogenesis. Notably, Adrenate presents dual biological effects: it transmits immune-protective signals but exerts direct vascular cellular toxicity. Our findings highlight the utility of MR-assisted precision toxicity prediction for disease risk evaluation and therapeutic target mining for AA.

papers.title: Causal Inference from Self-controlled Case Series
papers.abstract: The self-controlled case series (SCCS) design is widely used in studies of rare events, for example of vaccine side effects. Conceptually, the design has two main features. First, it requires only data from individuals who have experienced the event of interest. Therefore, the design is especially useful when the outcome is rare and the available data come from surveillance or clinical records, say, of hospitalized patients. Second, because comparisons are made within single individuals, time-invariant confounding between treatment and outcome is eliminated. We formulate a set of sufficient identification assumptions for estimating the causal effect of vaccination on an adverse outcome under the SCCS design, drawing on ideas from the causal inference literature. Unlike the existing SCCS literature, we do not consider a parametric model as the starting point. This allows us to establish when and why the SCCS design allows identification of causal effects, using data from cases only. However, because the sufficient identifiability assumptions are implausible in some applications, we also develop statistical tests for the existence of a treatment effect that remain valid when only a subset of the identification assumptions holds.

papers.title: High-Dimensional Off-Policy Evaluation without Sample Splitting using an Onsager Correction
papers.abstract: Reward models used for off-policy evaluation (OPE) are commonly selected using held-out data. When sample size and context dimension grow proportionally, the difference in test risk between models fitted on the full sample and on a fixed fraction of it need not vanish. Held-out evaluation can therefore consistently estimate the test risk of the model trained on the smaller sample, but because the relative ranking of candidate reward models can change after full-data refitting, held-out selection can be suboptimal. We develop an Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion that estimates the full-data reward model's out-of-sample risk under the target policy using only its training observations. This enables early stopping along the full-data gradient-descent trajectory without sample splitting. For neural networks with fixed depth and hidden width under Gaussian contexts, single-index rewards, context-dependent multi-index target policies, and known context-independent logging, we prove uniform consistency of our criterion over a fixed finite set of gradient-descent iterates and a near-oracle guarantee for the selected reward model. The same correction yields a doubly robust estimator that consistently estimates the true policy value without sample splitting, even when reward-model prediction error does not vanish. Experiments show decreasing risk-estimation error as dimension grows at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio, and improved reward-model selection relative to held-out baselines. Empirically, our correction also reduces the root mean squared error of doubly robust value estimates computed from the same data used to fit and select the reward models.

papers.title: Breaking Point: When Hidden Confounding Flips Off-Policy Evaluation
papers.journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
papers.abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) is used to decide whether a treatment policy learned from hospital records deserves a prospective trial, and every standard estimator assumes that the records contain everything the clinicians acted on. This report studies what happens when they do not, on the sepsis simulator of Oberst and Sontag (2019), extended with a hidden variable whose strength is set exactly. Because the simulator is ported to an exact transition tensor, the true value of every policy, the confounding strength Γ* under the marginal sensitivity model, and the infinite-data limit of every estimator are computed rather than estimated. The strength of confounding alone does not determine whether OPE recommends a worse policy. With infinite data, the estimators prefer withholding antibiotics, which is truly worse than the clinicians' policy, from Γ* = 12 when the hidden variable also worsens outcomes directly, and at no Γ* up to 152 when it harms only untreated patients. With 10,000 episodes, weighted importance sampling and a model-based estimate make this recommendation in 84% and 70% of datasets at Γ* = 12. With 2,000 episodes or fewer, the finite-sample biases of these two estimators, which have opposite signs, are as large as the confounding bias. Sharp sensitivity bounds at the true Γ* cover the true value in 96% to 99.9% of confounded datasets with 10,000 episodes, but a breakdown-point alarm calibrated on recorded variables fires on 86% to 100% of deploy decisions, with a precision no better than the base rate of wrong decisions.

papers.journal: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
papers.abstract: LLM agents increasingly rely on reinforcement learning to improve multi-turn reasoning, tool use, and environment interaction. However, existing training pipelines often treat an agent trajectory as a flat token sequence or a reconstructed message trace, making it difficult to preserve rollout fidelity, manage long contexts, and inspect step-level credit signals. We present Agent-R1, an open-source modular framework for agentic reinforcement learning (RL). Agent-R1 uses interaction steps as the native unit for trajectory representation, replay, and environment interaction, and decouples exact trajectory storage from flexible context construction. The system supports context-management policies, step-level rollout inspection, action-mask visualization, tool-feedback analysis, and unified comparison of related RL algorithms. Through demonstrations on multiple tasks, Agent-R1 enables users to configure, train, inspect, and compare agentic RL workflows within a single interactive interface. Code and project resources are available at https://github.com/AgentR1/Agent-R1.

papers.title: Learning from Unreachable Rewards: Hint-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning for Generative Recommendation
papers.journal: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
papers.abstract: Semantic-ID generative recommenders represent each item as a short sequence of discrete semantic tokens and predict the next item by autoregressively generating this token sequence. This paradigm enables a unified generation interface for item IDs, histories, and item text, but it also creates a structured optimization bottleneck during reward-based post-training: when an early semantic token enters the wrong branch of the item-token space, finite rollout groups rarely reach the ground-truth item, so group-relative optimization receives identical zero rewards and produces no useful advantage. We propose Hint-Conditioned Generative Recommendation (\method), a semantic-ID generative recommendation framework that recovers learning signal for such hard training instances. HCGRec diagnoses each instance with checkpoint rollouts and supplies a minimal target-prefix hint only when the current generator cannot reach the correct item. The model then generates the unhinted suffix under the hinted semantic branch, turning zero-reward groups into informative comparisons over item-token completions. Hinting also changes token identity: hinted prefix tokens are oracle-provided item context, while unhinted suffix tokens are sampled generation actions. We therefore introduce hint-aware credit decomposition, using supervised learning to preserve item-semantic and prefix-structure alignment for hinted tokens and GRPO to optimize the sampled suffix. Experiments on sequential recommendation benchmarks show that HCGRec substantially improves over supervised fine-tuning and vanilla reward-based post-training, while reducing zero-advantage training samples from over 70% to below 20%. The code is accessible at https://github.com/WncFht/GRec.

papers.title: The impact of temporal resampling on the safety of clinical reinforcement learning: A simulated trial

author_details.name: Steve Harris
affiliations: University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a type of artificial intelligence for making optimal choices. In healthcare, researchers generally use offline RL (ORL), where models are trained and evaluated from retrospective observational data. To accommodate naturally irregular clinical records, researchers often resample the data into uniform time intervals before training (known as binning). However, binning may create counterfactual trajectories that do not represent clinical practice. We first quantified these distortions in patients receiving continuous insulin infusions in the MIMIC-IV intensive care database. Binning reversed the apparent causal order for over 70% of paired glucose measurements and insulin adjustments within the same interval, and frequently masked significant dysglycaemic events and merged distinct treatment decisions together. We then conducted an in silico clinical trial using 30 virtual patients with type 1 diabetes from the FDA-approved UVA/Padova simulator. The simulator was modified to include stochastic intervals between decisions and used to generate a training dataset for offline RL. We trained three ORL algorithms on both the unprocessed dataset and equivalent datasets resampled at 10-minute, 2-hour, and 4-hour intervals. When deployed back into the simulated environment, temporal resampling was found to reduce model performance by up to 60% relative to unprocessed data, with 4-hour binning causing all agents to perform worse than the dataset's baseline. Retrospective evaluation on resampled data actively obscured this effect, predicting 1.5-3x better returns than agents achieved in practice. We recommend that future research in this area prioritises datasets with natural clinical timings between decisions, which may be a necessary step before these models can be safely deployed into patient care.

papers.title: SPyCE: Skill-Policy Co-evolution for Multimodal Agents

author_details.name: Weijie Qiu
affiliations: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications

papers.journal: ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM)
papers.abstract: Multimodal agents that think with images iteratively manipulate visual evidence and invoke tools across many steps. Existing reinforcement learning methods reduce trajectories to scalar rewards, forcing the policy to discover reusable tool-use patterns from scratch on every new task; memory-based alternatives retain past experience, yet they rely on test-time retrieval, without updating the policy to absorb reusable patterns from that experience. Our key insight is that multimodal reasoning trajectories should be distilled into reusable skills that co-evolve with the policy during training, rather than being consumed as rewards or retrieved from a static store. To this end, we propose SPyCE (Skill-Policy Co-evolution), a framework that distills trajectories into a hierarchical skill library and updates it throughout reinforcement learning. Execution skills capture local visual operations, while workflow skills encode high-level priors that orchestrate tool use. During training, the policy model conditions on retrieved skills to guide its rollouts, while the skill library evolves using valuable rollouts generated by the policy. This creates a closed loop in which improved policies yield better skills, and the evolving skill library, in turn, provides stronger priors for policy rollouts. Experiments across eight benchmarks demonstrate that SPyCE consistently outperforms both RL-based and memory-based baselines. Further analysis reveals that both the hierarchical skill design and the co-evolution mechanism are critical to our design. These results suggest joint skill-policy optimization as a promising paradigm for building capable multimodal agents.

papers.title: R 2 -Searcher: Calibrating Retrieval and Reasoning Boundaries for Agentic Search
papers.journal: ACM International Conference on Information and Knowledge Management (CIKM)
papers.abstract: Recent search agents for multi-hop reasoning often fail by either retrieving incomplete evidence or reasoning over irrelevant portions of the retrieved content, leading to a retrieval-reasoning boundary shift. We propose R 2 -Searcher, a novel framework that explicitly explores and calibrates the retrieval and reasoning boundaries via fine-grained, query-token-guided evidence modeling and post-retrieval reflection. Specifically, R 2 -Searcher: (1) constructs fine-grained reasoning contexts by extracting precise facts from retrieved content based on query token semantics (e.g., subjects, actions, temporal markers, and degree modifiers), thereby guiding the attention of search agent; (2) introduces a retrieval reflection mechanism that evaluates and corrects boundary deviations after each retrieval step, guiding the generation of improved queries grounded in the extracted reasoning contexts; and (3) employs an end-to-end reasoning-reflection-guided reinforcement learning algorithm, R 2 PO, which jointly optimizes both boundaries through a tree-based exploration of reasoning regions and reflections. Our method significantly enhances the quality of both retrieval and reasoning, establishing an iterative loop where retrieval and reasoning mutually enhance each other. Extensive experiments on seven complex multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that R 2 -Searcher significantly outperforms state-of-the-art agentic search methods in answer accuracy and retrieval-reasoning quality. Ablation studies further confirm the critical role of retrieval-reasoning boundary calibration. Implementation code is available for reproducibility: https://github.com/Applied-Machine-Learning-Lab/CIKM2026_R2-Searcher.

papers.title: A Separation Principle for Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) problems in which agents evolve under decoupled noisy dynamics but share a population objective. A canonical example is a mobility operator that orchestrates a fleet of vehicles to meet customer demand. The stochastic and time-varying nature of these problems calls for learning approaches, yet existing MARL algorithms do not scale: learning assignment and routing jointly over the full state-action space becomes prohibitive as the number of agents grows. Formulating the problem over the space of probability measures, we prove a separation principle: the population cost-to-go function is upper bounded by an optimal transport problem whose transportation cost is the target-conditioned single-agent cost-to-go function. This simplifies the multi-agent problem to learning a single-agent policy and coordinating the agents via optimal transport. Building on this principle, we introduce SALT (Separation-based Assignment and Learning via optimal Transport), a family of algorithms that learn a target-conditioned single-agent policy using any standard reinforcement learning algorithm, and then coordinate the agents via optimal transport. Since learning occurs at the single-agent level, SALT scales to fleet sizes where MARL baselines become intractable and transfers without retraining to fleet sizes unseen during training. In a vehicle-delivery experiment on the southern Manhattan road network, where MARL baselines are computationally prohibitive, SALT improves travel time by 15-21% over a shortest-path routing heuristic. In stochastic grid worlds, SALT reduces average travel times by 23-61% relative to MARL baselines and scales to population sizes where these methods fail.

papers.title: CARGO: Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Preventive Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Cooperative Driving
papers.abstract: This study presents Causal Attribution and Responsibility-Guided Optimization (CARGO), a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for cooperative on-ramp merging in mixed traffic. A shared latent-context posterior and an action-conditioned response model estimate directed behavioral influence, with posterior uncertainty propagated into interaction-edge selection. Complementary attribution mechanisms couple signed influence with marginal team utility for cooperative reward shaping and assign responsibility from positive excess tail risk relative to a safe reference policy. Conditional diffusion generates future responses for action-dependent risk estimation. Responsibility-guided preventive optimization calibrates agent-specific risk-reduction requirements to local capacity within a policy trust region, using reserved safety margins, adaptive requirement scaling, and joint feasibility verification. Theoretical analysis establishes risk monotonicity and sufficient local conditions for non-decreasing environmental return under explicit assumptions. Experiments in highway-env across three traffic densities, together with controlled graph-recovery and attribution studies, support the effectiveness of the framework. Under high-density traffic, CARGO increases the success rate by 66.04\% and reduces the crash rate by 56.23\% relative to the best evaluated baseline for each metric.

papers.title: HM-CDSS: A Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Framework with Conservative Q-Learning and Retrieval-Augmented Clinical Reasoning for Sepsis Decision Support

author_details.name: Madeha Arif
affiliations: National University of Sciences and Technology

author_details.name: Usman Qamar
affiliations: King Fahd University of Petroleum and Minerals

author_details.name: Soyiba Jawed
affiliations: National University of Sciences and Technology

papers.abstract: Decision-making in healthcare in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) is a very complex and multi-dimensional process. Sepsis management requires well-coordinated, simultaneous decisions across vasopressor titration, fluid restoration, antibiotic supervision, and haemodynamic monitoring, each operating on different physiological timescales. Despite advances in reinforcement-learning-based clinical decision support, existing systems treat these as a single flat action space and cannot capture the multi-level structure of real clinical reasoning. Moreover, most systems lack explainability mechanisms, making them unsuitable for accountable clinical practice. This study proposes the Hierarchical Multi-Agent Clinical Decision Support System (HM-CDSS), a four-phase hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework designed to address these limitations. Using a cohort of 5,282 adult ICU sepsis patients from the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV) database, approximately 78,200 offline trajectory transitions are constructed. A single-agent Dueling DQN baseline achieves a mean test reward of 4.385 but exhibits conservative policy collapse, reaching only 10.3% clinician agreement. The proposed Hierarchical Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (HMARL) system introduces a meta-agent that assigns high-level clinical goals to four specialist sub-agents trained with Conservative Q-Learning (CQL), using agent-specific regularization weights (α = 1.0 for vasopressor and fluid agents; α = 0.5 otherwise) to prevent out-of-distribution Q-value overestimation. A three-condition ablation study confirms that CQL adds 21.8% points of clinician agreement above a hierarchical DQN baseline, and that hierarchy and distributional constraint are complementary mechanisms. Overall clinician agreement reaches 49.9%, a gain of 39.6% points over the single-agent baseline. Additionally, a retrieval-augmented generative reasoning layer, based on Sepsis-3 and Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines, produces chain-of-thought clinical justifications evaluated through a proposed five-metric framework comprising Guideline Grounding Score, Hallucination Rate, Clinical Consistency Score, Recommendation Completeness, and Uncertainty Calibration (UC; note that UC could not be computed empirically in the current evaluation due to uniformly high agent confidence). Across 98 evaluated timesteps, the system achieves 0% hallucination and 100% recommendation completeness across the 98-timestep evaluation sample; these results should be interpreted as preliminary, given the limited sample size. HM-CDSS proposes an integrated framework combining offline hierarchical MARL, guideline-based explainability, and quantified reasoning-quality assessment for ICU clinical decision support.

papers.title: SEER: A Scalable Event-Driven Runtime for Parallel Execution of Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Environments
papers.abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is increasingly used in systems where many entities interact in a shared environment. In these workloads, policy inference can be batched on GPUs, but the CPU-side environment path still updates entity states, resolves local interactions, and builds observations inside each $\mathrm{env.step}$. This path can dominate latency in interaction-intensive workloads after policy batching. Existing vectorized environment interfaces and general event-driven runtimes do not directly address the fine-grained cross-entity work inside one bounded MARL step while preserving the step-level semantics expected by learning systems. We present SEER (Scalable Event-Driven Environment Runtime), a runtime for MARL environment execution under an explicit event-locality contract. SEER models each environment step as a bounded stream of timestamped events. If direct state updates are entity-local and cross-entity effects are represented as ordered future events, SEER can run independent events in parallel while preserving serial-equivalent boundary outputs. To make this contract practical, SEER uses a CAS-based dual-layer event queue: local event queues preserve per-entity causal order, while a parallel executive list exposes ready work to global worker threads. SEER further uses STPA, a preflight-guided thread-pool selection mechanism that combines short runtime traces with static workload and hardware features. We evaluate SEER on two parameterized MARL workloads: compute-intensive UAV swarm control (Aircraft) and communication-intensive wireless management (PCS). On Aircraft, SEER reduces inference latency by 16.2\% over the baseline. On PCS, SEER reduces environment-execution latency by 46.9\%, 19.5\%, and 64.9\% over ROSS-T, NBSE, and ROOT-Sim, respectively.

papers.title: Regulating Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand Operators with Fixed and Adaptive Penalties: A Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach
papers.abstract: Profit-maximizing Autonomous Mobility-on-Demand (AMoD) operators may exploit consumer surplus through excessive prices and underserve less profitable regions by relocating vehicles away from them. We study how penalty-based regulation of an AMoD operator in a multimodal mobility system can limit surge pricing and improve regional service availability. We model regulation as an outer control loop that acts on a learning-based operator. Static regulation with fixed penalties is formulated as a Markov Decision Process for an operator that jointly controls pricing and rebalancing, and dynamic regulation as a Partially Observable Stochastic Game in which a regulator periodically adjusts region-specific penalties in closed loop. Operator and regulator policies are learned with graph-based multi-agent reinforcement learning. In experiments with real-world Manhattan data, fixed surge pricing penalties reduce the share of travelers facing excessive prices from 22% to 1%. For regional service availability, dynamic regulation improves the regulator's reward by up to 15.6% over fixed penalties of equal mean intensity. The gains in service availability are strongest when spare fleet capacity exists, whereas service deficits persist in peak periods with highly utilized fleets. The learned regulator policy responds by reducing penalties where limited fleet capacity restricts compliance. The results identify trade-offs between regulatory targets, operator profitability, and traveler utility.

papers.title: Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning via Epigraph-Form Guided Exploration
papers.abstract: Discovering cooperative behavior in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is challenging due to the combinatorial complexity of joint state-action spaces, which hinders the emergence of coordinated behaviors from trial-and-error alone. Intrinsic rewards are often used to aid discovery, but naively combining them with team objectives can distort the learning signal, compromising task performance. In this paper, we propose EFXPLORER, a constrained exploration framework that maximizes exploration objectives subject to a constraint that preserves established task performance. We solve the resulting problem using an epigraph reformulation that introduces adaptive exploration budgets. This approach separates intrinsic rewards from task objectives and regulates exploration through task feasibility. To further encourage diverse and temporally extended exploration, we incorporate a successor distance-based intrinsic reward that captures long-horizon dependencies. Empirically, our method outperforms strong baselines and induces novel cooperative strategies across SMAX, VMAS, and MPE benchmark suites.

papers.title: H^2MARL: Hierarchical Heterogeneous Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning for Humanoid Robot Control
papers.abstract: Coordinated whole-body control of humanoid robots remains challenging due to high-dimensional coupled dynamics and substantial physical heterogeneity across joint degrees of freedom (JDoFs). Existing multi-agent reinforcement learning methods either employ coarse agent partitions or directly apply generic heterogeneous-agent algorithms, while hierarchical controllers commonly optimize high-level planning and low-level execution independently, leading to uncoordinated motion. In this paper, we propose H^2MARL, a hierarchical heterogeneous multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with two key mechanisms. We first formulate humanoid whole-body control using a JDoF-level physical-heterogeneity-aware policy factorization, where each torque-actuated JDoF is conditioned on an explicit descriptor of its actuation, kinematic, and dynamic properties. Moreover, we develop a closed-loop policy-executor co-optimization mechanism that jointly adapts the high-level pose planner and the low-level joint executor using shared interaction trajectories, thereby reducing the distribution mismatch between planning and execution. Extensive experiments in MuJoCo and Isaac Gym demonstrate that H^2MARL consistently improves locomotion stability, gait coordination, and motion quality over homogeneous, coarse-grained, and independently optimized alternatives.

papers.title: Adaptive reconstruction mechanism for enterprise collaborative networks based on multi-agent reinforcement learning
papers.abstract: Enterprise collaborative networks must reorganise as markets shift, partners fail and demand changes. This study develops an adaptive reconstruction mechanism in which each firm acts as an autonomous agent that adds, terminates or reweights collaborative ties within a bounded candidate set. The Multi-Agent Deep Q-Network with Prioritized Experience Replay (MADQN-PER) combines attention-based coordination, a dynamic learning rate and rewards that mix firm-level and network-level objectives. Graph operations have explicit enterprise meanings, authorising parties and cost components; action masks enforce feasibility before selection. Across synthetic networks of 50 to 200 nodes, the reported efficiency gains range from 34.7% to 41.2%, with 78.3% performance retention under 15% random node failures. Attention and the shared reward are associated with the largest component differences in composite score. A calibrated supply-chain simulation reports a 41.7% reduction in delivery time and a 53.2% robustness gain. Quantitative comparisons are restricted to the five baselines with documented configurations. Conservative bounds derived from ten-run summaries distinguish gains in efficiency, robustness and adaptability from the reconstruction-cost trade-off. The evaluation schedule supports finite-budget comparisons but does not establish convergence times.
